claims.text: Protective oxide formation and retention in high-temperature HEAs is controlled by slowed diffusion of major alloying elements inherent to the high-entropy effect.
Slowed diffusion forces selective oxidation of reactive elements such as Cr or Al.
Selective oxidation occurs uniformly at the alloy surface.
Selective oxidation of Cr or Al produces a thin, continuous, and adherent Cr2O3 or Al2O3 scale.
The resulting protective scale retards further oxidation.
The proposed initial HEA has a uniform distribution of multiple principal elements, including Cr or Al.
The controlled comparison varies reactive-element concentration in otherwise compositionally similar HEAs and oxidizes them for the same duration at 900–1100°C.
Protective oxide formation is typically thermodynamically favorable above 800°C and below the temperature at which oxide instability or spallation occurs.
Oxide-scale uniformity and adhesion are mediated by slowed diffusion and uniform reactive-element distribution in the HEA.
Reduced diffusion of the principal constituents confines oxidation to selected reactive elements at the surface.
Controlled selective oxidation rapidly forms an ultra-thin, self-healing oxide layer.
The ultra-thin oxide layer impedes oxygen ingress and subsequent scale growth.
Increasing reactive-element concentration will produce a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scale than in a lower-reactive-element baseline HEA.
Increasing reactive-element concentration will lower oxidation kinetics and weight gain relative to the baseline.
A lower-reactive-element baseline is expected to form a thicker and less uniform oxide layer with faster oxidation kinetics.
The hypothesis applies in air at 800–1100°C when Cr2O3 or Al2O3 is thermodynamically stable and is less applicable outside that range or in non-oxidizing atmospheres.
Failure of the higher-reactive-element samples to show consistently thinner, more uniform, more adherent scales and lower weight gain would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The reactive species are described as minor elements in the hypothesis but as included among the multiple principal elements in the stated initial alloy.
